appraisal_events.evidence: "Gilberte était persuadée maintenant qu'elle n'était pas allée à Tansonville... pour fuir les Allemands... mais au contraire pour les rencontrer et défendre contre eux son château," while "on parlait dans les journaux avec les plus grands éloges de son admirable conduite et il était question de la décorer."
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator exposes Gilberte's self-flattering revision of her own 1914 motives for going to Tansonville, quietly undercutting her sincerity, even as he reports that the press genuinely praised her wartime conduct and floated decorating her.

appraisal_events.evidence: "Tel j'abordai Robert qui avait encore au front une cicatrice plus auguste et plus mystérieuse pour moi que l'empreinte laissée sur la terre par le pied d'un géant," amid the narrator's description of returning soldiers as touched by something supernatural and death-adjacent.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator elevates Saint-Loup by framing his war scar and presence in near-mythic, sacred terms, marking him as transformed by his proximity to death at the front.

status_effects.explanation: The narrator's exposure of her self-serving rewriting of her 1914 departure casts a shadow of vanity over her self-presentation.
Independent of the narrator's irony, the press publicly praised her wartime conduct and raised the possibility of decorating her, marking a real gain in public esteem.
Saint-Loup is strongly elevated in the narrator's regard through the reverent, quasi-mythic description of his war scar and his aura as a man returned from the brink of death.

ambiguities: It is unclear whether the press's praise of Gilberte's conduct is meant to be read as independently earned or as tinged by the same ironic distance the narrator applies to her self-serving revision of her departure story.
